IMS Tutorials

Package website: https://ppbds.github.io/ims.tutorials/

About this package

ims.tutorials is a collection of tutorials, one per chapter, accompanying Introduction to Modern Statistics by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. Students work through each chapter’s ideas in R, using AI to build an analysis in their own Quarto document. Built with learnr2: each tutorial is a Quarto document rendered to a static web page.

Installation

Install the development version from GitHub with:

remotes::install_github("PPBDS/ims.tutorials", dependencies = TRUE)

This also installs the development version of learnr2 and every package the tutorials use, including the book’s data packages, openintro and usdata. Rendering a tutorial requires the Quarto CLI.

Tutorials

The recommended way to launch tutorials is with the R Tutorials extension for VS Code, which lists every installed tutorial and lets you start one with a click.

As a backup, you can launch a tutorial from the R console with learnr2::run_tutorial(), providing the short name of the tutorial and the package name.

learnr2::run_tutorial(name = "hello-data",
                     package = "ims.tutorials")
  • Hello Data (“hello-data”). Chapter 1: the stent experiment, cases and variables in loan50, associations among US counties, and experiments versus observational studies.
  • Study Design (“study-design”). Chapter 2: populations and samples, and simple random, stratified, and convenience sampling with mlb salaries; random assignment, blinding, and placebos with the stent experiment; confounding in county.
  • Applications: Data (“applications-data”). Chapter 3: getting to know paralympic_1500, and Simpson’s paradox in 1500m gold medal times.
  • Exploring Categorical Data (“exploring-categorical-data”). Chapter 4: contingency tables, bar plots, and conditional proportions in loans_full_schema, and comparing county incomes across groups.
  • Exploring Numerical Data (“exploring-numerical-data”). Chapter 5: histograms, shape, and summary statistics for loan50, and transformations and intensity maps of county.
  • Applications: Explore (“applications-explore”). Chapter 6: keeping plots simple, using color to draw attention, and telling a story with the chapter’s company expenses and Duke hiring data, then order, labels, purpose, and color with its Brexit poll.
  • Linear Regression with a Single Predictor (“linear-regression-single”). Chapter 7: fitting a least squares line, residuals, correlation, R-squared, a two-level categorical predictor, and outliers, with possum, elmhurst, and mariokart.
  • Linear Regression with Multiple Predictors (“linear-regression-multiple”). Chapter 8: indicator and categorical predictors, many predictors, adjusted R-squared, and backward and forward selection, modeling interest rates in loans_full_schema.
  • Logistic Regression (“logistic-regression”). Chapter 9: callback rates in the resume hiring experiment, the logit, logistic models with one and many predictors, predicted probabilities, and groups of different sizes.
  • Applications: Model (“applications-model”). Chapter 10: a case study of house prices in duke_forest, from correlation and a one-predictor model to a multiple regression chosen by backward elimination.
  • Hypothesis Testing with Randomization (“hypothesis-testing-randomization”). Chapter 11: hypotheses, randomization tests, null distributions, p-values, and statistical discernibility, with the sex_discrimination and opportunity_cost experiments.
  • Confidence Intervals with Bootstrapping (“confidence-intervals-bootstrap”). Chapter 12: bootstrapping a proportion and bootstrap percentile confidence intervals, with the chapter’s medical consultant and tappers-and-listeners case studies, and a simulation of what 95% confidence means.
  • Inference with Mathematical Models (“inference-mathematical-models”). Chapter 13: the Central Limit Theorem, the normal model, standard errors, and normal-based tests and intervals, checked against simulation, with opportunity_cost and stent30.
  • Decision Errors (“decision-errors”). Chapter 14: two-sided tests, Type 1 and Type 2 errors, the discernibility level, and power, simulated on the cpr blood-thinner experiment.
  • Applications: Foundations (“applications-foundations”). Chapter 15: a randomization test on the 20-volunteer malaria vaccine trial, malaria, comparing data, randomization, and bootstrap distributions.
  • Inference for a Single Proportion (“inference-for-a-single-proportion”). Chapter 16: the bootstrap test for a proportion and the normal model (success-failure condition, confidence intervals, Z test), with the chapter’s medical consultant and payday loan polls.
  • Inference for Comparing Two Proportions (“comparing-two-proportions”). Chapter 17: randomization tests, bootstrap intervals, and the normal model for a difference in proportions, with pooled and unpooled standard errors, using cpr, fish_oil_18, and mammogram.
  • Inference for Two-Way Tables (“inference-two-way-tables”). Chapter 18: expected counts, the chi-squared statistic, a randomization test of independence, and the chi-squared distribution, using ask and diabetes2.
  • Inference for a Single Mean (“inference-single-mean”). Chapter 19: bootstrap and t-distribution intervals and a t-test for a mean, using the chapter’s sample of 100 runners from run17.
  • Inference for Comparing Two Independent Means (“comparing-independent-means”). Chapter 20: randomization tests, bootstrap intervals, and the t-distribution for a difference in means, using classdata, stem_cell, and births14.
  • Inference for Comparing Paired Means (“comparing-paired-means”). Chapter 21: paired data, randomization within pairs, bootstrap intervals, and the paired t-test, using UCLA Bookstore and Amazon textbook prices in ucla_textbooks_f18.
  • Inference for Comparing Many Means (“comparing-many-means”). Chapter 22: ANOVA by randomization test on the F statistic and by the F distribution, using classdata and on-base percentage by position in mlb_players_18.
  • Applications: Infer (“applications-infer”). Chapter 23: the redundant-adjectives experiment, with a bootstrap interval for one mean, a paired randomization test, and tests for two independent means, each checked against the t-distribution.
  • Inference for Linear Regression with a Single Predictor (“regression-single-inference”). Chapter 24: randomization tests and bootstrap intervals for a slope, then the t-test, t-interval, and model conditions, using births14, midterms_house, and elmhurst.
  • Inference for Linear Regression with Multiple Predictors (“regression-multiple-inference”). Chapter 25: regression output with many predictors for loans_full_schema, multicollinearity, and cross-validation with penguins.
  • Inference for Logistic Regression (“logistic-regression-inference”). Chapter 26: inference for logistic regression coefficients, model diagnostics, and cross-validation of spam models, using email.
  • Applications: Model and Infer (“applications-model-infer”). Chapter 27: a case study of Mario Kart auctions in mariokart, with regression output, a permutation test and bootstrap for a slope, and cross-validation.
